items.item: a queue message, consumed and acknowledged against a real on-disk database, is genuinely gone when asked for again; a log message survives a consumer's own offset rewind and is read again unchanged

at.step: Reveal: replay is the real dividing line

items.item: The hook's own two outcomes are not an arbitrary design choice between two systems; they follow directly from what each system's own acknowledgement protocol is defined to do, which is exactly what the predict step is built to surface before the reveal names the mechanism.

at.step: Hook: the identical message, delivered two ways: a queue acknowledges and it's gone, a log advances a marker but keeps it

items.item: A queue's own negative-acknowledgement requeue is not the same thing as a log's replay, even though both result in a message being seen again: a requeue happens because the original delivery was never successfully acknowledged, while a log's replay can happen for a message that was already successfully consumed once.

at.step: Reveal: a queue deletes on acknowledgement

items.item: A log's own offset being a single rewindable integer, rather than a per-message deletion flag, is what makes the storage itself cheap to keep: tracking consumption state costs one number per partition regardless of how many messages exist, which is a different trade-off than a queue's own per-message bookkeeping.

at.step: Reveal: a log tracks a position, not a deletion

items.item: Replay being possible is a direct consequence of the log never deleting on read, not a separately bolted-on feature; any system that keeps a message's own position permanent and lets a reader's own position move independently gets replay for free, which is why Kafka's own documentation can describe it as violating 'the common contract of a queue' rather than as a special case.

at.step: Reveal: replay is the real dividing line

items.item: Fan-out and ordering are two separate real properties that happen to both favor the log for a related reason: partitioning is what gives per-partition ordering, and the same partitioning (plus never deleting on read) is what lets many independent consumer groups each read the whole stream without interfering with each other.

at.step: Reveal: ordering and fan-out tilt the choice further

items.item: Share groups blurring the queue/log line doesn't make the distinction this topic draws obsolete; it adds a third real option (per-record acknowledgement on a log) rather than replacing either of the first two, which is exactly why the 'Prove it' step's own correct answer is still a plain offset-based log, not share groups specifically.

at.step: Reveal: Kafka's own share groups blur the line

items.item: This topic's own lab measurement uses a real on-disk database rather than an in-memory structure deliberately, because the deletion in the queue table and the offset update in the log table are both genuine, committed writes — the same durability guarantee a real broker's own acknowledgement and offset-commit protocols rely on, not an in-memory approximation of it.

This topic establishes which structure gets a consumer to its data (a queue or a log); it says nothing yet about structures that trade correctness itself for a massive reduction in memory, which is exactly the shift the next topic makes by opening the chapter's closing section on approximate structures.

The 'Prove it' step's own scenario combines fan-out and replay deliberately, not redundantly: a workload that only needed fan-out could still work with enough queue consumers added, and a workload that only needed replay could work with a single-consumer log, but needing both at once is what rules out the queue entirely.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: This topic's own log-offset material is the same structural idea this chapter's earlier write-ahead-log topic already introduced one layer down: an append-only record addressed by a position that never changes, reused here at the level of an entire messaging system instead of a single database's own durability mechanism.
